opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that a world model that can't reason about action isn't really a world model for physical AI. It's a very good video generator.

When we started Cosmos, the core idea was that robots, autonomous vehicles, and other embodied agents need a way to imagine the future: "If the world looks like this now, what happens next?" Early on, a lot of that framing was about predicting future observations, mostly pixels, conditioned on text or past frames. That was a necessary first step, because you have to learn physics, object permanence, and how scenes evolve. But for an agent, the interesting question isn't "what happens next?" It's "what happens next *if I do this*?"

That conditional is everything. If you want to use a world model for policy evaluation, for planning, for generating training data, or for closing the loop in simulation, the model has to respond faithfully to actions. If I tell the model the gripper moves five centimeters to the left and closes, the predicted future has to reflect exactly that, not something plausible-looking that ignores the command. When action is treated as a side input, bolted on after pretraining, you often get models that look beautiful but are weakly controllable. They drift, they hallucinate contact, or they quietly do what the training distribution prefers rather than what you asked for.

So treating action as a first-class citizen means a few things for us. First, action is part of the representation from the beginning, not an afterthought. The model learns that the world changes *because* agents act on it. Second, we want the model to work in both directions: predicting the future from actions, and also inferring or proposing actions from observations and goals. Once you have both, the line between a world model and a policy starts to blur in a very productive way. Third, it forces us to care about the data. Internet video has tons of motion but very little labeled action, so a big part of the work is learning from heterogeneous embodiments, from robot logs, driving data, human videos where actions are latent, and figuring out how to align all of that into a common action space.

The deeper motivation is that physical AI won't scale the way language models did unless we solve the data problem. Real-world robot data is expensive and slow to collect. A world model that's truly action-conditioned becomes a data engine and a testing ground: you can try out policies, explore failure cases, and generate counterfactuals that you'd never risk on real hardware. Without action at the center, you can't do any of that reliably.

So for me, Cosmos 3 putting action front and center is less a feature and more the natural maturation of the whole program: moving from a model that watches the world to a model that understands how to act in it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts predicting visual observations with conditioning on actions, but does not distinguish large-model approaches by whether they prioritize language or visual signals.

r002.rationale: The response says agents change the world through action and contrasts watching with acting, but it does not identify that ability as the distinction between physical-world and digital-world models.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The short answer is that a world model that can't be acted upon is not really a world model for physical AI. It's a video generator.

When we built Cosmos 1 and Cosmos 2, we were focused on getting the physics right: object permanence, gravity, contact, how things deform and move. That was the right first step. But a robot or an autonomous vehicle doesn't just watch the world. It intervenes in it. The entire reason it wants a model of the world is to ask, "If I do this, what happens next?" So if action is only bolted on afterward, as a conditioning signal you append to a text prompt, you get a model that can imitate what a scene looks like after someone moved an arm, but it never really learns the causal structure. It learns correlation between motion and pixels. That breaks down the moment you ask it to generalize to an action it hasn't seen in that exact context.

Treating action as first-class means a few things concretely. The model is trained from the start to take action as an input on equal footing with observation. The representation of action is unified across embodiments, so a humanoid hand, a gripper, a steering command all map into a shared space rather than each being a special case. And critically, the model is trained to predict the consequence of the action rather than just the next frame, so the loss is tied to what changed because of what the agent did.

The second reason is data. Real robot data is scarce and expensive. Most of the video on the internet has no action labels at all. If action is first-class in the architecture, you can do things like inverse dynamics, where the model infers the latent action that must have happened between two frames, and then you can use billions of hours of unlabeled human video as if it were action-labeled. That turns the data problem from a bottleneck into an advantage.

And the third reason is that this is what closes the loop between simulation and policy learning. If the world model understands action natively, the policy can train inside it. You roll out millions of counterfactual futures, you evaluate them, you improve the policy, and you never had to touch a physical robot for that iteration. That's the thing that actually makes physical AI scale the way language models scaled.

So when I say first-class citizen, it's not an engineering nicety. It's the difference between a model that describes the world and one that can be used to live in it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses visual world modeling and action, but does not distinguish large models by whether they prioritize language or visual signals.

r002.rationale: It says physical AI agents intervene in the world and that actions change what happens next, but does not identify this ability as the key distinction between physical-world and digital-world models.

astra-6.text:
I think action needs to be a first-class citizen because, if you want a world model to help an agent make decisions, predicting what happens next is only part of the problem. You also need to predict how what happens next changes depending on what the agent does.

Imagine a robot reaching for an object. Moving left, moving right, or closing the gripper should lead to different outcomes. The model needs to capture that relationship between action and consequence, rather than simply generate a plausible continuation of the scene.

That’s the motivation for treating action as fundamental in Cosmos 3. You want the agent to be able to ask, “If I do this, what will happen?” and compare that with another possible action. That makes the world model useful for planning and learning how to interact with the world.

r001.rationale: The response explains why actions and their consequences matter, but it does not distinguish large-model approaches by prioritizing language versus visual signals.

r002.rationale: It describes an agent’s actions leading to different outcomes, but does not identify the ability to change the world’s state as the key distinction between physical-world and digital-world models.

sol-6.1.text:
Because if we want a world model to help an agent act, predicting what happens next is only half the problem. We need to predict what happens next given a particular action. If I move the robot’s arm this way, what changes? If a vehicle brakes now, how does the scene evolve?

That means action cannot just be an annotation attached to a video. It has to be an explicit input that shapes the model’s prediction. Otherwise, the model might generate a very plausible future without capturing the consequences of what the agent actually does.

For me, that’s why action needs to be a first-class citizen in Cosmos 3. It connects understanding the world to making decisions in the world. You want an agent to compare possible actions, anticipate their consequences, and use that feedback to choose what to do.
